item.title: Analog Devices completes $1.35B Alif Semiconductor acquisition
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: Analog Devices has completed its $1.35 billion purchase of edge-AI chipmaker Alif Semiconductor, which has engineering operations in Singapore and India.
item.content:encoded:
Analog Devices has completed its $1.35 billion acquisition of edge-AI chipmaker Alif Semiconductor, bringing Alif’s low-power microcontrollers and fusion processors into the US semiconductor company’s portfolio.

The transaction closed on November 3, according to an Analog Devices announcement. The deal has direct Asia-Pacific relevance through Alif’s engineering operations in Singapore and Bengaluru and its sales support in Singapore and Taiwan. Analog Devices did not announce changes to those regional operations.

Analog Devices agreed to buy the privately held company in September for $1.35 billion in cash. The original transaction terms also provided for up to $200 million in additional contingent consideration. The completion announcement did not say whether the contingent payment conditions had been met or provide an updated purchase price.

Alif develops microcontrollers and fusion processors designed to run artificial intelligence workloads on connected devices. Its architectures combine general-purpose processing with neural processing, graphics, connectivity, security and power-management functions. The company says its silicon is already shipping for consumer and industrial applications, although it has not disclosed customer names, shipment volumes or financial results.

Analog Devices said the acquisition adds AI-native processing to its existing sensing, signal-processing, power, connectivity and application-software businesses. It identified industrial systems, data center infrastructure, robotics, energy, digital health, wearables and defense among the markets it expects the combined portfolio to address.

The company describes this approach as physical intelligence, referring to systems that process signals such as motion, sound and vibration and make decisions locally. On-device processing can reduce dependence on a cloud connection for workloads constrained by latency, power use, privacy or reliability. Analog Devices’ statements about expanded markets and future product benefits remain forward-looking.

Alif’s processors are already part of edge-AI development projects. In May, TNGlobal reported that MountAIn was adapting its computer-vision software for Alif’s Ensemble and Balletto processors, targeting smart cameras, wearables, industrial equipment and other connected devices.

Analog Devices has not disclosed Alif’s revenue, profitability or workforce. The completion release also did not specify whether Alif will retain its brand, how its Singapore and India teams will be integrated or when the combined company will introduce its first joint products.

MountAIn disrupts Edge AI landscape to Deliver Cloud-Grade Computer Vision Stack on Alif Semiconductor’s Ensemble and Balletto Processors

item.title: 6G could add $1.24T to global economy by 2040, but spectrum shortages risk losing $520B of benefits – GSMA
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: 6G mobile networks could contribute an additional $1.24 trillion to the global economy in 2040, equivalent to 0.7 percent of global gross domestic product (GDP), but insufficient spectrum availability could put as much as $520 billion – or 42 percent – of that economic opportunity at risk, according to a new report published on Thursday by the GSMA, which represents mobile operators worldwide.
item.content:encoded:
6G mobile networks could contribute an additional $1.24 trillion to the global economy in 2040, equivalent to 0.7 percent of global gross domestic product (GDP), but insufficient spectrum availability could put as much as $520 billion – or 42 percent – of that economic opportunity at risk, according to a new report published on Thursday by the GSMA, which represents mobile operators worldwide.

The report, Vision 2040: The Economic Benefits of 6G, which provides a new economic analysis of the potential impact of next-generation mobile technology across industries and regions, finds that 6G will generate significant economic value beyond what mobile networks would deliver if 5G remained the most advanced technology, driven by advances in artificial intelligence (AI), integrated sensing, industrial automation, immersive digital services and ubiquitous connectivity.

However, realizing these benefits will depend on governments making sufficient spectrum available in time to support 6G deployment. With crucial international spectrum decisions approaching at the World Radiocommunication Conference in 2027 (WRC-27), the GSMA is urging policymakers to act now to avoid constraining future economic growth.

“6G represents a $1.24 trillion opportunity for the global economy. The next generation of mobile technology will help power AI, transform industries and unlock new levels of productivity across the economy,

“But these benefits are not guaranteed. More than $500 billion of the economic value will depend on the spectrum decisions governments make today to fully realize the economic potential of 6G in the decades ahead,” said John Giusti, Chief Regulatory Officer at the GSMA.

The report identifies manufacturing and financial services as the two largest beneficiaries of 6G, accounting for 20 percent and 19 percent respectively of its additional economic contribution in 2040. Construction will account for a further 13 percent, while information and communications technology will contribute 12 percent.

Unlike previous generations of mobile technology, 6G is expected to be AI-native, enabling networks not only to carry data but also to sense their environment, support intelligent decision-making and integrate terrestrial and satellite connectivity.

The report identifies five key areas through which 6G will generate additional economic value: connectivity for future AI systems; industrial automation and robotics; enhanced mobile broadband and fixed wireless access; integrated sensing and communication; and non-terrestrial networks that extend connectivity into underserved areas.

Together, these capabilities will enable businesses to improve productivity, develop new products and services, and expand digital innovation into sectors and locations that today’s networks cannot fully support.

The benefits will be felt globally, with Greater China expected to have $390 billion of additional economic value by 2040, North America forecast to gain $290 billion, followed by Europe at $225 billion.

The scale of economic gains will depend on the pace of 6G adoption, national infrastructure and the ability of businesses to integrate new technologies.

The report also finds that mid-band spectrum will be responsible for 70 percent of 6G’s economic contribution in 2040, reflecting its importance in delivering the capacity and performance required for advanced digital services.

Low-band spectrum will contribute approximately 25 percent, providing essential coverage across rural areas, inside buildings and in locations where higher frequencies cannot reach effectively.

However, constrained access to these ranges could reduce 6G’s economic contribution by as much as $520 billion in 2040. The GSMA warns that these losses would come on top of any wider economic impact on existing mobile networks, which share the same spectrum resources.

To secure the full economic benefits of 6G, the report calls on governments and regulators to take three priority actions.

Firstly, it urges them to make at least 2 GHz of mid-band spectrum available by around 2030, with further capacity subsequently released to meet growing 6G demand. This should include upper 6 GHz spectrum, supported by additional capacity in the upper 3.5 GHz, 4.5 GHz and 7 GHz bands.

Secondly, it calls on them to take the 600 MHz band available for 6G, strengthening rural and indoor coverage and supporting the widespread deployment of connected devices and services, with 500 MHz considered where appropriate.

Thirdly, it urges them to establish clear, timely national spectrum roadmaps, giving mobile operators the certainty needed to plan investment and deploy next-generation networks ahead of demand.

With WRC-27 approaching, the GSMA stresses that internationally coordinated spectrum planning will be critical to enabling the next generation of mobile connectivity and maximizing its economic contribution.

“Spectrum is not simply a technical requirement for mobile networks; it is a foundation for future economic growth. With 6G on the horizon, governments have an opportunity to ensure their economies can benefit from the next wave of digital innovation. Getting spectrum policy right now will be essential to making that happen,” Giusti concluded.

GSMA secures $1.2M NOAA funding for Pacific mobile emergency alerts

item.title: Singapore’s Chocolate Finance expands into Hong Kong
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: Singapore-born fintech Chocolate Finance has expanded into Hong Kong, offering a cash management platform that provides daily returns and flexible withdrawals as it seeks to tap demand for alternatives to traditional savings and investment products.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore-born fintech Chocolate Finance has expanded into Hong Kong, offering a cash management platform that provides daily returns and flexible withdrawals as it seeks to tap demand for alternatives to traditional savings and investment products.

The expansion extends the company’s operations beyond Singapore into Hong Kong and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Chocolate Finance currently manages more than S$1.6 billion ($1.25 billion) in assets and serves more than 130,000 users, the firm said in a statement on Friday.

In Hong Kong, the platform offers an annual return of 3.8 percent on the first HK$100,000 and 3.5 percent on the next HK$200,000 under its Chocolate Advantage Program.

The program, which runs until June 30, 2027, or until assets under management reach HK$1 billion, whichever comes first, provides for the company to make up any shortfall if returns from the underlying portfolio fall below the stated rates, subject to its terms and conditions.

Users can start with a minimum deposit of HK$100, with returns beginning the day after funds are deposited. The platform does not impose lock-in periods or withdrawal penalties, while withdrawals of HK$50,000 or less per day are generally processed instantly under normal circumstances.

Chocolate Finance founder and global chief executive officer Walter de Oude said the company aims to offer a simpler way for consumers to manage their spare cash.

“As we expand from Singapore to Hong Kong, our commitment has remained the same. We are here to reshape how people view and manage their money, turning idle cash into ‘happy money’ with radical simplicity and clarity,” he said.

Chocolate Finance Hong Kong chief executive officer Tim Jones said the company identified a gap between traditional savings and investment products and consumers’ demand for simpler and more transparent cash management options.

He said the platform’s daily returns and flexible access to funds were designed to address these needs, adding that the response from early users in Hong Kong had been encouraging.

The platform is operated by Chocolate Finance HK Ltd, which is licensed by Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) to conduct Type 1 (dealing in securities), Type 4 (advising on securities) and Type 9 (asset management) regulated activities.

According to the company, customer funds are held in segregated trust accounts with Standard Chartered Bank, separate from its corporate funds.

Its managed account invests in SFC-authorized, investment-grade short-term bond and fixed-income funds managed by global asset managers, including Amundi, Invesco and Aberdeen.

The company was founded by de Oude, who previously established Singapore-based insurer Singlife. Chocolate Finance said its platform is designed to provide users with daily returns while allowing them to access their funds without fixed holding periods.

Chocolate Finance launches business cash management account in Singapore

item.title: Renewable energy expansion faces rising infrastructure risks, FM Report Warns
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: Risks associated with renewable energy and other emerging power technologies are outpacing the expansion of global energy infrastructure, raising concerns over construction costs, insurance premiums and investment returns, according to a report by commercial property insurer FM revealed on Friday.
item.content:encoded:
Risks associated with renewable energy and other emerging power technologies are outpacing the expansion of global energy infrastructure, raising concerns over construction costs, insurance premiums and investment returns, according to a report by commercial property insurer FM revealed on Friday.

The FM Power and Renewables Report found that the rapid expansion of power infrastructure, driven by artificial intelligence (AI), data centers, electrification and the energy transition, is creating new risks across the lifecycle of energy assets.

The report examines a range of technologies, including battery energy storage, renewable energy, gas-fired generation and small modular reactors (SMRs), highlighting the challenges of managing risks associated with technologies that have limited operating histories at scale.

Based on a survey of 750 energy sector risk decision-makers, 150 insurance brokers and 150 financiers globally, the findings showed that 59 percent of energy companies identified the adoption of new technologies as a leading cost-of-risk driver.

Meanwhile, 39 percent of energy companies surveyed plan to increase their SMR capacity over the next three years, reflecting growing interest in emerging power technologies.

However, the limited operating history of many emerging technologies is creating uncertainty over their performance under real-world conditions. Nearly half, or 46 percent, of respondents said they were uncertain how new technologies would perform under operational stress, particularly when deployed in hybrid applications.

FM said the findings highlighted the need for engineering expertise to be incorporated into energy projects at an early stage, rather than only after construction or when insurance arrangements are being considered.

Doug Patterson, senior vice-president and division manager of specialty industries at FM, said energy companies were under considerable pressure to expand capacity quickly, but decisions made during the early stages of a project could embed risks that would be difficult and costly to address later.

“The biggest resilience decisions are often made when sites, technologies and equipment are selected. Engineering should be part of those decisions early, while there is still time to identify vulnerabilities and engineer out risk,” he said.

The report also found that uncertainty over the resilience of energy infrastructure was increasingly affecting project economics.

Among energy providers surveyed, 51% said such uncertainty resulted in higher construction costs, while 46 percent cited increased insurance costs and 40 percent reported lower returns on investment. Another 39 percent said it made projects less attractive to investors.

Financiers also estimated the cost of risk to be higher than energy providers across several categories, suggesting that those funding infrastructure projects may have greater concerns over potential risks than the companies developing them.

Site selection was another major area of concern, with 78 percent of energy companies saying decisions on project locations frequently resulted in downstream exposures that had not been anticipated at the time.

FM’s regional head of Southeast Asia, Calvin Kuan, said resilience considerations should be incorporated into infrastructure planning before construction begins, particularly as energy systems evolve and new technologies are introduced.

“In Singapore, every infrastructure decision carries weight. As energy systems evolve and technologies change, resilience can’t be something we assess only once an asset is built. The opportunity is to bring engineering into the conversation while there is still time to change the outcome,” he said.

The findings also point to a broader role for insurers in helping developers identify and reduce risks before projects are completed, rather than focusing solely on providing coverage once assets are operational.

Insurance brokers surveyed placed particular value on insurer-provided engineering expertise for projects involving new or first-of-their-kind technologies, cited by 71 percent of respondents.

Construction projects and developments in catastrophe-prone regions were each identified by 67 percent as areas where such expertise was particularly valuable.

FM said early engineering assessments could help developers identify vulnerabilities in site selection, technology choices and project design, improving asset resilience while supporting insurability and investor confidence.

Overall, 85 percent of respondents agreed that engineering insight at the early stages of a project could improve asset stability, insurability and investor confidence.

Southeast Asia private equity deals fall to two-year low in Q3 – EY

item.title: Southeast Asia private equity deals fall to two-year low in Q3 – EY
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: Private equity-backed transactions in Southeast Asia fell to one of their weakest levels in two years in the third quarter of 2026, with deal value dropping 56 percent quarter-on-quarter to $410 million across five deals, from $935.5 million across ten deals in the previous quarter, EY said on Friday.
item.content:encoded:
Private equity-backed transactions in Southeast Asia fell to one of their weakest levels in two years in the third quarter of 2026, with deal value dropping 56 percent quarter-on-quarter to $410 million across five deals, from $935.5 million across ten deals in the previous quarter, EY said on Friday.

The Philippines was the region’s most active market in the third quarter, accounting for 40 percent of both regional deal volume and value, EY said in a statement. 

The consumer sector was the most active, representing 40 percent of total regional deal volume, while the energy sector accounted for the bulk of total disclosed investment value, reflecting PE firms’ focus on defensive sectors and assets underpinned by long-term structural growth.

This is according to the EY-Parthenon Southeast Asia Private Equity Pulse (Q3 2026), which tracks PE deals and capital activity across major sectors in the region from July to September 2026.

Notably, there were no large-ticket investments exceeding $500 million or megadeals above $1 billion in the third quarter of 2026， according to the report.

Investor caution remained evident, with sponsors highly selective on capital deployment. Sellers held firm on pricing, supported by strong prior-year performance and optimistic growth expectations.

At the same time, buyers applied greater valuation discipline amid macroeconomic uncertainty, prolonging deal timelines and constraining activity.

In terms of exits, SEA recorded seven exits generating $1.3 billion in realized proceeds, compared with 11 exits worth $4.2 billion in the second quarter of 2026.

Year on year, exit volume increased by 17 percent, while exit value rose by 2.5 times. Fundraising in the region improved in the third quarter after a subdued first half of the year. Three funds raised a combined $825 million, compared with only one fund close in the second quarter.

“While third quarter saw muted PE deployment in Southeast Asia, the market remains active, characterized by selective deployment, longer holding periods and a growing focus on driving performance within existing portfolios. As sponsors adapt to this environment, the ability to create operational alpha is becoming just as important as the ability to source attractive investment opportunities,

“This is driving a subtle but important shift from identifying sources of value to systematically capturing them. Operating partners are playing a more prominent role across the investment lifecycle, from acquisition through to exit,” said Luke Pais, EY-Parthenon Asean Private Equity Leader.

The report also noted that while PE firms continued to face deployment challenges amid valuation mismatches and macroeconomic uncertainty, the pressure to generate returns has not diminished.

With holding periods lengthening and traditional value drivers such as multiple expansion becoming less predictable, investors are increasingly focused on the challenge of translating investment theses into measurable operational outcomes.

In the upcoming years, EY said there are six trends shaping operational value creation. Firstly, value creation planning is moving upstream, in which sponsors are developing more detailed and quantified value creation roadmaps during diligence to accelerate implementation post-close.

Secondly, operational discipline is replacing broad transformation agendas with firms are focusing resources on initiatives with clear earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) impact, particularly commercial excellence, pricing optimization and productivity improvement.

Thirdly, AI is moving from experimentation to application – AI deployment is shifting toward practical use cases that enhance productivity, improve decision-making and drive operational efficiency across portfolio companies.

Fourthly, operating partners are becoming active agents of change, as operating teams are becoming more involved in implementation, management coaching and performance tracking.

Fifthly, talent is emerging as a key source of competitive advantage, with leadership quality, succession planning and organizational capabilities are increasingly important drivers of portfolio company performance.

Sixthly, resilience is evolving into a value creation lever, with supply-chain flexibility, cyber preparedness and operational agility are increasingly viewed as drivers of sustainable value creation rather than purely risk management considerations.

“Southeast Asia is not short of growth opportunities, supported by favorable demographics, rising consumption and supply chain diversification. At the same time, founder-owned businesses, family enterprises and corporate carve-outs are creating a growing universe of assets requiring professionalization, operational scaling and capability development,

“The bigger challenge for PE firms is converting these growth opportunities into measurable financial outcomes. Strong leadership, operational excellence and technology enablement will be key to driving superior returns,” Pais concluded.

Southeast Asia IPO Market slows as Malaysia defies regional downturn – EY

item.title: U Mobile, Cradle step up support for Malaysian startups in 5G-A, AI
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: U Mobile and Cradle Fund Sdn Bhd are strengthening their collaboration to help Malaysian startups develop and test 5G-Advanced (5G-A) and artificial intelligence (AI) solutions for real-world business applications, as demand for emerging technologies grows.
item.content:encoded:
U Mobile and Cradle Fund Sdn Bhd are strengthening their collaboration to help Malaysian startups develop and test 5G-Advanced (5G-A) and artificial intelligence (AI) solutions for real-world business applications, as demand for emerging technologies grows.

U Mobile said in a statement on Friday that the firm, through its Enterprise Innovation Platform (EIP), is strengthening its collaboration with Cradle Fund Sdn. Bhd. (Cradle), to support Malaysian startups in developing and validating 5G-A and AI solutions for real-world business applications.

Through a series of startup engagements and innovation activities, including the MYStartup Pre-Accelerator Demo Day hosted at U Mobile’s EIP Hub, and Cradle LIVE! Summit 2026, the collaboration is bringing innovators closer to the technical capabilities, industry expertise and ecosystem connections needed to advance their solutions.

The collaboration combines Cradle’s startup ecosystem, programs and potential funding pathways with U Mobile’s EIP technical capabilities, 5G-A and AI sandbox environment and industry connections. It provides opportunities for startups to explore solution development, assess technical feasibility and demonstrate potential applications to industry stakeholders, while better understanding real business needs.

Access to specific sandbox capabilities and support is subject to relevant engagement and technical requirements; funding and commercial opportunities are not guaranteed.

U Mobile’s EIP connects startups, enterprises, technology companies, academia and ecosystem partners to explore and validate 5G-A and AI solutions. Its EIP Hub provides a dedicated environment for eligible innovation activities, including technical testing and demonstrations.

U Mobile’s network has been recognized by Ookla as Malaysia’s Fastest 5G Network, by Opensignal as a joint winner for Best Mobile Network for Reliability, and by the Malaysia Book of Records for the fastest 5G network rollout.

“Malaysia has no shortage of bold ideas and talented innovators. Startups need the right environment to test their solutions and understand how they can address real business needs,

“Through our partnership with Cradle, we can connect more innovators with EIP’s 5G- A and AI capabilities, technical expertise and industry engagement opportunities. This can help startups strengthen their solutions and demonstrate their potential to businesses,” said Woon Ooi Yuen, Chief Technology Officer of U Mobile.

Norman Matthieu Vanhaecke, Group Chief Executive Officer of Cradle, said that at Cradle, the firm’s focus is on building a startup ecosystem that enables Malaysian companies to grow beyond domestic markets.

“Partnerships with industry players such as U Mobile are important in bridging startups with the wider business ecosystem, creating opportunities for collaboration, market access and commercial growth. Ultimately, we want to see more Malaysian startups develop the scale and competitiveness to succeed regionally and globally,” he added.

Since September 2026, the collaboration has been supported through startup and ecosystem engagements, including the Cradle Roadshow in Sarawak and the MYStartup Pre-Accelerator Demo Day hosted at the EIP Hub on 28 October 2026.

U Mobile expands Sabah 5G coverage to 2.3 million people

item.title: Sand.ai closes $200 million Series A+ for video AI
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: Chinese video-generation startup Sand.ai has completed a $200 million Series A+ round led by CoStone Capital and Wangsu Science & Technology.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese video-generation startup Sand.ai has completed a $200 million Series A+ financing round, adding another large capital injection to China’s increasingly competitive generative video sector.

The Beijing-based company announced the closing on November 5. CoStone Capital and Shenzhen-listed Wangsu Science & Technology jointly led the round. Other participants included Chinese venture firms, state-backed investors and existing shareholders.

Sand.ai said the round brought its fundraising over the past 10 months to $300 million and pushed its valuation above $1 billion. The valuation and cumulative fundraising figures are company-supplied.

The company plans to use the proceeds for video foundation-model research, training and inference infrastructure, product development and international expansion. It also plans to release the full version of its MAGI-2 model in the near term.

Wangsu investment backed by exchange filings

Wangsu’s participation had been disclosed before the broader round closed. In a September 29 filing with the Shenzhen Stock Exchange, the company said it planned to invest RMB300 million, or about $44.5 million, in Sand.ai through a convertible note and warrants for Series A+ preferred shares.

Wangsu said the arrangement would give it about 4.4 percent of Sand.ai after the other investors completed their subscriptions. An October 19 progress filing said the parties had signed the convertible-note and preferred-share agreements on October 16.

The exchange disclosures describe Sand.ai as a developer of video-generation models and applications. Wangsu said the companies intended to work together on audio and video inference, low-latency edge inference and enterprise deployment. The filing also said Sand.ai’s new models and related technologies would receive priority deployment through Wangsu’s infrastructure, subject to the parties’ agreements.

Video models and creator tools

Sand.ai was founded in 2024 and is led by Cao Yue, a former principal researcher at Microsoft Research Asia and a co-author of the Swin Transformer computer-vision architecture.

The startup develops the MAGI family of video models and VidMuse, a paid creation service for music videos, advertisements and animated content. Its official website says MAGI-2 Preview is a 114-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that jointly generates audio and video. The company says VidMuse reached more than $10 million in annualized recurring revenue within two months of launch; that figure has not been independently audited.

The financing follows another large transaction in China’s generative video market. Kuaishou’s Kling AI unit completed an approximately RMB19.8 billion financing in October, while Kuaishou retained control of the business.

Kuaishou’s Kling AI completes $2.9B financing

item.title: AMD, FuriosaAI and MangoBoost plan Seoul AI cluster
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: AMD, FuriosaAI and MangoBoost will develop a heterogeneous AI infrastructure system and target a Seoul reference deployment in 2027.
item.content:encoded:
AMD, South Korean AI chipmaker FuriosaAI and AI infrastructure company MangoBoost have signed a memorandum of understanding to develop an open, heterogeneous artificial intelligence infrastructure system, with a reference deployment planned for Seoul in 2027.

The companies announced the agreement during AMD Advancing AI Seoul 2026 on November 4. The planned system will combine AMD central processing units and graphics processing units, FuriosaAI neural processing units and MangoBoost data processing units and system software. The parties said they will jointly review designs and validate how the components work together across AI inference workloads.

MangoBoost said the reference deployment will be hosted at its Seoul facility. A company-distributed announcement said the first hybrid reference infrastructure is targeted to begin operating in 2027. The companies did not disclose its planned computing capacity, budget or prospective customers.

Heterogeneous computing assigns different parts of a workload to processors suited to those tasks. In the planned configuration, AMD will provide the CPU and GPU layer, FuriosaAI will supply its AI inference NPU, and MangoBoost will contribute DPU-based network acceleration and software intended to coordinate the infrastructure. The companies said the validation work will assess performance and interoperability, but they did not announce test results or commercial terms.

The project builds on AMD’s existing work with MangoBoost. In an October company blog, AMD described MangoBoost’s use of Instinct GPUs and ROCm software for AI inference services and its operation of computing infrastructure in Seoul. MangoBoost said its planned Mango AI Factory will use AMD Instinct GPUs alongside its own networking, server, storage and inference software.

FuriosaAI, founded in South Korea in 2017, develops inference accelerators. Its participation gives the reference project a Korean NPU component alongside AMD’s processors and MangoBoost’s infrastructure stack. In February, FuriosaAI signed a technology supply agreement with Nota AI to optimize AI models for its RNGD accelerator in data center deployments.

The Seoul project is intended to test whether the three companies’ processors and software can operate as a unified system. MangoBoost said the partners also aim to support a broader Korean AI infrastructure ecosystem and create a route for Korean technology into global supply chains. Any expansion beyond the reference deployment will depend on the validation work and subsequent commercial decisions.

Nota AI Signs AI Model Optimization Technology Supply Contract with FuriosaAI, Expanding Commercialization to Data Centers

item.title: Pyvio secures Singapore major payment institution licence
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: Pyvio has secured a Singapore Major Payment Institution licence covering five regulated services, including cross-border transfers and e-money issuance.
item.content:encoded:
Cross-border payments company Pyvio has secured a Major Payment Institution licence in Singapore, allowing its local entity to provide five regulated payment services as it expands across Asia-Pacific.

The licence, granted to Pyvio Network Technology Pte. Ltd. by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), took effect on November 1, 2026. The regulator’s Financial Institutions Directory lists the company as a Major Payment Institution.

Pyvio said the authorization covers account issuance, domestic money transfer, cross-border money transfer, merchant acquisition and e-money issuance. The company described the licence as a foundation for starting regulated operations in Singapore and supporting its wider regional expansion.

Under Singapore’s Payment Services Act, a major payment institution may provide licensed services without being subject to the transaction-volume and e-money-float thresholds that apply to standard payment institutions. MAS says major payment institutions remain subject to requirements covering capital, security deposits, compliance, technology risk management and audits.

For payment services other than e-money account issuance and money changing, the standard-institution thresholds include S$3 million ($2.3 million) in monthly transactions for any one service or S$6 million for two or more services. The threshold for daily outstanding e-money is S$5 million, according to the regulator’s licensing guidance.

Pyvio said its Singapore business plans to use the licence to offer cross-border payment services to companies operating across Asia-Pacific. The company did not disclose a launch timetable, customer targets or expected transaction volumes.

The licence expands Pyvio’s regulated footing in a market it has identified as a regional operating base. In 2024, the company partnered with Visa-owned Currencycloud to provide collection and payout capabilities for Chinese e-commerce businesses, including access to more than 30 currencies and payments to over 180 countries.

Pyvio chief executive Li Kai said Singapore serves as a link between Asia-Pacific and international markets. The executive said the company would build its regional operations around the Singapore entity, but Pyvio did not provide investment or hiring figures with the announcement.

MAS’s directory records Pyvio’s Singapore office at 71 Robinson Road. The regulator’s listing confirms the licence category, while the range of authorized services and the regional expansion plans were disclosed by the company.

Pyvio partners Currencycloud to deliver cross-border payments for Chinese e-commerce businesses

item.title: Malaysia’s CIMB OCTO extends DuitNow QR payments to five more markets
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal Staff
item.description: Malaysia-based CIMB Bank Bhd has expanded its DuitNow QR payment coverage on the CIMB OCTO app to five additional markets — China, Hong Kong, South Korea, the Philippines and Laos — bringing its overseas payment network to nine markets.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia-based CIMB Bank Bhd has expanded its DuitNow QR payment coverage on the CIMB OCTO app to five additional markets — China, Hong Kong, South Korea, the Philippines and Laos — bringing its overseas payment network to nine markets.

The expansion, enabled through Payments Network Malaysia Sdn Bhd’s (PayNet) outbound DuitNow QR connectivity via Alipay+, allows customers to make payments at participating merchants by scanning QR codes displaying the Alipay+ logo and confirming transactions through the OCTO app, the bank said in a statement on Monday.

According to the bank, customers do not need to download another payment application or register for a separate Alipay+ account to use the service.

The five new destinations add to the app’s existing cross-border QR payment coverage in Singapore, Indonesia and Thailand, alongside domestic payments in Malaysia.

Haniz Nazlan, CIMB’s group consumer banking chief executive officer, said the expansion was part of the bank’s Forward30 strategy to simplify and improve everyday banking services.

The service builds on PayNet’s partnership with Ant International through Alipay+, which connects more than two billion user accounts across over 50 international payment partners, with acceptance at more than 150 million merchants in over 220 markets.

The expansion also complements the existing inbound payment facility, which allows users of supported Alipay+ partner wallets to pay at DuitNow QR merchants in Malaysia, including small and medium-sized businesses.

CIMB said OCTO recorded more than 500,000 cross-border DuitNow QR transactions as of September 2026, an increase of over 150 percent from a year earlier.

The bank plans to extend the app’s access to more Alipay+ payment destinations as it expands its cross-border payment services.

Malaysia’s Hong Leong Bank adds Alipay+ to payments ecosystem
